articles.title: Modi to visit Manila for ASEAN Summit; maritime security, trade on agenda
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will travel to Manila on Monday (November 16, 2026) for a three-day visit to attend the annual India-ASEAN summit that is expected to focus on boosting maritime security cooperation and enhancing trade and investment ties.
He will also attend the annual East Asia Summit. Philippines is hosting the summits in its capacity as the current chair of the 11-nation ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations).

Mr. Modi is also set to join Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, U.S. President Donald Trump, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for the annual Quad summit in Manila. There is, however, no official word on the Quad summit.
At the India-ASEAN and the East Asia summits, New Delhi is expected to pitch for deeper maritime cooperation among the like-minded nations in the Indo-Pacific.
The ASEAN is considered one of the most influential groupings in the region, and India and several other countries including the U.S., China, Japan and Australia are its dialogue partners.

"Prime Minister Modi will be travelling to Manila to attend the 23rd ASEAN-India summit and the 21st meeting of the ASEAN-led East Asia Summit process. The visit will take place from November 16 to 18," said Rudrendra Tandon, Secretary (East) in the External Affairs Ministry.

He said Mr. Modi's programme in Manila will include attending a dinner to be hosted by the President of the Philippines Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for the visiting dignitaries of this summit process and bilateral meetings.
Mr. Modi will attend the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit process on November 17.
The top official said enhancing maritime security and trade and investment ties will be among the key focus areas at the Summit.

The East Asia Summit is the premier forum in the Asia-Pacific region to deal with issues relating to security and defence. Since its inception in 2005, it has played a significant role in the strategic, geopolitical, and economic evolution of East Asia.
Apart from the ASEAN member states, the East Asia Summit includes India, China, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Australia, New Zealand, the U.S. and Russia.
"There is also a very strong demand from the Indian community to meet the Prime Minister. So we are trying to adjust that also in his schedule," Mr. Tandon said at a media briefing.

articles.title: India undergoing massive transformation in renewable energy: Earthshot Prize CEO
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: India is at the forefront of climate solutions, and its innovations have immediate global application, especially when it comes to issues such as heat stress, Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf said. He was speaking with The Hindu on Thursday (November 12, 2026) on the background of the launch of the five-day Earthshot Prize summit, which will take place in Mumbai and Jaipur from November 13 to 17.

As COP31 gathers in Türkiye for climate negotiations, it is India and Mumbai which will send a message of climate solutions, he said. “There is a race going on right now. The first country that can have access to cheap, clean and abundant energy, is going to have a huge economic advantage. And I think, India knows that. Which is why so much is being done here to use the huge solar resource that India has,” he said.

Earthshot Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious environmental awards. It was founded by Prince William six years ago. This is the first time the awards are being held in India. Prince William will be in India for the events.

On Thursday (November 12, 2026), Mr. Knauf spoke about how India was an inspiration behind starting the award, why the awards are being held in India and particularly in Mumbai this year, and the lessons he has learnt during his stay in the country. Observing that India is undergoing a “massive transformation” about renewable energy, he said it had an advantage over other countries to bring in sustainable climate solutions. He said there was no debate between economic progress and environmental protection anymore. “What is good for the environment is good for business, and Indian companies are showing that,” Mr. Knauf said, adding that the past Indian winners had been able to raise $800 million in commercial international investment after winning the Earthshot Prize.
The Earthshot Prize is slated to make large announcements about two Indian finalists — Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and Mahila Housing Trust, in the coming week.

Mr. Knauf said climate action conversation needed to move beyond the ‘environment bubble’. Acknowledging India’s efforts in the conservation sector, he said it was important to showcase India’s optimism to the world. Adding that the inspiration behind the awards came from India too, he spoke of how the Prince of Wales saw environmental action during his visit to India in 2016, when he was inspired by the country’s approach towards working with nature.

“For a country that is on the frontline of the environmental issues despite having not caused them, people are more optimistic about their abilities to solve them, than many richer countries. That tells you something. We all have to learn from that example. We are happy that the Earthshot Prize is coming here to celebrate that Indian spirit for the whole world,” Mr. Knauf said. He added that Mumbai was chosen as it was the financial and entertainment capital of the country.

“Earthshot Prize is about getting out to people. We want to get out to investors, to corporate leaders. We also want to tap into the world of entertainment and sporting. Mumbai is the perfect place for that. It is the global capital for the financial sector and the entertainment world,” he said.

This year, Earthshot Prize ceremony will be held at an unprecedented scale, he said, adding that over 5,000 people would participate in the events which would draw people from different countries, and children from over 24 States of India. The event would be live telecast around 240 countries for the first time.

Asked about how he saw the climate challenge, Mr. Knauf said he was an eternal optimist. “At Earthshot, we have a simple equation — urgency + optimism = action. Anyone who wants to give up and be negative, that is a big threat to action. As big a threat as carbon emissions. Because the second we decide that the issues are too hard, then we look the other way. That is giving up, and particularly for the next generation that is coming, it is an unacceptable attitude,” he said.

articles.title: ISRO successfully carries out ground static test of PSLV third stage
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) which is looking to get its workhorse launcher, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), back on track has successfully carried out the ground static test of the PSLV third stage (PS3) at the Static Test Facility in Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

“Subsequent to the anomalies observed in the third stage of PSLV during the PSLV-C61/EOS-09 & PSLV-C62 / EOS-N1 missions, the configuration of the PS3 stage was revisited comprehensively with respect to the design margins, raw material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures, and the quality checks that were followed so far,” ISRO said.

“The configuration has been strengthened and essential improvements have been carried out in the nozzle configuration to improve design margins along with updated procedures in the acceptance of raw materials, assembly procedures and quality checks,” ISRO added.
It also said that the mechanical interfaces have been strengthened with redundancy in the sealing systems and adequacy of the design margins have been verified.

“The updates in assembly procedures and non-destructive tests (NDT) during the various phases of integration and transportation have been implemented and the new version of the PS3 solid motor stage is realised and tested successfully,” ISRO said.
Based on the detailed analysis and reviews of the test data, the space agency said further tests are planned.

articles.title: Study suggests not all obesity means ill-health
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Only between a quarter and a third of people currently diagnosed with obesity should be considered as in poor health, according to a new study that joins calls to overhaul how the condition is diagnosed.

The study, published in Nature on Wednesday, follows a proposal last year from experts and medical organisations to move obesity diagnosis beyond just body mass index (BMI), based on a person’s weight and height, to include body fat and broader health.

The study attempts to show what this new definition could mean for diagnosis levels, prevalence, and ultimately, treatment, for a condition the World Health Organization currently estimates affects more than one billion people globally.

Obesity can be a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease and cancer. The study suggests defining it as pre-clinical, when the condition is largely a risk factor, and clinical, when it is causing ill health.

Using data from almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the study estimates that under the new framework, 1% to 3% of those defined as obese using BMI alone would not be, while another 5% to 9%, with higher body fat for example, would be diagnosed with the condition. Across a population, this could affect tens of millions of people.
The study’s senior author Francesco Rubino, professor and chair of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London, said the inaccuracy of BMI measurements was well-known.

“But we haven’t so far got a better system,” he said. That is what the new framework aims to do, he added, saying it could “provide a meaningful clinical characterisation of obesity that can inform care and policy.”

The new framework proposes measuring body fat, including by waist circumference, as well as BMI, and considering if a patient has any organ dysfunction linked to weight, like heart or liver problems, before making a diagnosis.

This means some people with high BMI alone would not be classed as having obesity. Those who have high body fat and high BMI would be diagnosed with “pre-clinical obesity”, and those who also have organ dysfunction would have “clinical obesity” – considered an active disease that would usually require more urgent treatment.
Under these criteria, only on average roughly 27% of people with obesity across the four studied countries have clinical obesity, the study estimated – representing around 8.5% of all adults.

The majority of those with “pre-clinical obesity” – around 82% on average across the four countries studied – did not progress to clinical obesity, although progression rates were higher in China and Spain, the study found.

articles.title: CAR-T trial deaths do not deter lupus patients hoping for a cure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.

“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.

Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.

Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.

What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.

In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.

Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.

articles.title: Milking power: On the overturning of Gokul Dairy cooperative mandate
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy , by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.

The Congress-backed Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi, led by Satej Patil, won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the Gokul board. On October 29, the election of the chairman was deadlocked after the BJP-allied members did not participate, and the meeting fell short of the required quorum of 14 members. The directors allied to the Congress and its partners subsequently declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar as chairman, but the administration refused to recognise the election as quorum requirements had not been met. The amendment made through the ordinance allowed the government to nominate five directors to certain large cooperative institutions, with four nominees receiving voting rights. To be sure, four were nominated immediately to the Gokul board, and they voted with the BJP and its partners to elect a chairman on November 10 . The mandate of the cooperative’s members had been 13-12 in favour of the Congress and its allies, but it turned 16-13 in favour of the BJP and its partners, with the appointment of members with voting rights by the State government. Those defeated approached the Bombay High Court on November 9 to restrain the government-nominated directors from voting, but the High Court did not grant that relief. The diffidence of the judiciary in intervening in favour of democratic principles is turning out to be a matter of concern . The overturning of the popular mandate in Gokul Dairy cannot be seen as an isolated incident. It is yet another instance in a troubling pattern of state power silencing the people’s choice.

articles.title: Visions of the future: On this year’s Booker Prize
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

articles.title: Caste and class: On OBC reservation
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: If public resources are to dismantle both caste hierarchy and class inequality, OBC reservation should resist the notion that caste disadvantage makes economic differences among OBC families irrelevant. The ‘creamy layer’ rules are responsible for identifying those OBC members who have advanced sufficiently to no longer require affirmative action. However, the government has implemented them inconsistently. The Supreme Court in March corrected one inconsistency, that the government cannot hold the salary alone of an OBC candidate’s parent as evidence of social advancement. In Indra Sawhney (1992) , the Court upheld the government’s 27% reservation for OBC candidates in central government services if it also excluded economically advanced sections, i.e., the creamy layer, among OBCs. Following the equivalence requirement issued in 1993, the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) issued a “clarification” in 2004 that the government used, from around 2015, to deny dozens of OBC candidates who had cleared the Civil Services Examination their benefits because their parents’ salaries exceeded the official threshold due to pay revisions that did not always reflect changes in occupational status. The Cabinet also approved equivalence guidelines in 2017 but a parliamentary committee criticised it over a number of issues.

In Rohith Nathan (2026) , the Court rightly rejected the government’s use of the 2004 “clarification” to arbitrarily exclude OBC candidates based on their parents’ salaries alone. However, the government stalled service allocations following the 2025 examination and appealed that retrospectively applying the ruling would create administrative chaos. On November 6, the Court conceded that it had not asked the government to reopen completed selections, as it could set workers against one another while leaving government misapplication unaddressed. A proactive policy is essential now as the government must create supernumerary posts for legitimate claimants and apply the 1993 rules to pending allocations without vouchsafing these remedies for only those who can afford litigation. Access to public employment continues to be grossly unequal: per the 2024-25 DoPT Annual Report, OBC representation in central government employment was 26.3% but declined steadily towards higher positions. As the Justice G. Rohini Commission also indicated, the benefits of reservation are distributed unevenly among OBC communities. However, the report, submitted in 2023, is still not in the public domain. The coming Census includes caste enumeration but policymakers also need data on each caste’s education, occupations, assets, and landholdings. Defending redistribution among caste groups while ignoring major inequalities within them, and constraining OBC reservation assuming relatively more high-income families capture the benefits without first establishing the extent and the causes are equally difficult to justify.

articles.title: Without any rationale: On the disbanding of the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: By abruptly disbanding the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee on Union-State Relations and handing over its task to the Tamil Nadu State Law Commission, the C. Joseph Vijay government appears to have succumbed to the political impulse to reverse earlier decisions rather than being guided by any compelling rationale or necessity. This gains credence from the very grounds cited. The committee executed its mandate with scholarly rigour, seen in Part I of its report that was submitted to the then M.K. Stalin government in February. Citing the Committee’s basic character of being a “non-statutory body” is unconvincing, particularly when the Law Commission itself is established only through “executive order”. There is also no public evidence of State Law Commissions having examined or addressed issues concerning Union-State relations. The mandate “to suggest ways and means for the inter-State relations and Centre-State relations”, constitutes only one part of the broader terms of reference of the State Law Commission, reconstituted in August. Given the commission’s wider responsibilities, successive State governments had constituted high-level committees to examine conflicts involving Concurrent List subjects and recommend specific remedies. It is through such recommendations that Tamil Nadu enacted certain pieces of legislation to overcome limitations imposed by central laws, including the provision of horizontal reservation in professional course admissions for disadvantaged students. Therefore, the State’s other argument of “similarity or overlap” in the “nature and scope of the functions” entrusted to the Committee and the Commission, does not withstand close scrutiny.

In September, Leader of the Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin, had flagged an attempt to “paralyse” the Committee’s functioning . A fair assessment of the Committee’s Part I Report reveals the breadth and depth of its dispassionate examination of issues, including State autonomy, delimitation, and the office of the Governor. Parties, barring the BJP, had largely welcomed the report. Interestingly, its contents are not even remotely at odds with the broad public ideological positioning of Mr. Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam on State rights. Besides, Prof. M. Naganathan, the Committee’s only member with an overt political association, had already resigned. The government would do well to rethink and allow it to complete its work. This would strengthen the political endeavour towards evolving a more balanced federal governance structure, facilitating harmonious Centre-State relations.

A fair assessment of the Committee’s Part I Report reveals the breadth and depth of its dispassionate examination of issues, including State autonomy, delimitation, and the office of the Governor. Parties, barring the BJP, had largely welcomed the report. Interestingly, its contents are not even remotely at odds with the broad public ideological positioning of Mr. Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam on State rights. Besides, Prof. M. Naganathan, the Committee’s only member with an overt political association, had already resigned. The government would do well to rethink and allow it to complete its work. This would strengthen the political endeavour towards evolving a more balanced federal governance structure, facilitating harmonious Centre-State relations.

articles.title: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The two Deepavali nights following the Supreme Court’s (SC) temporary relaxation of the cracker ban , played out predictably. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in several north Indian cities — already ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ in the first week of November — was ‘severe’ on Deepavali night . Several air sensors — maintained by various organisations — reported PM2.5 in Delhi and its outskirts, exceeding 1,000 by Deepavali night. In this context, the SC’s order last week regarding crackers bears revisiting. While stating it was aware of the consequences of emissions from crackers, the Court has been waiting for quantitative evidence on the health and environmental effects of emissions from Deepavali celebrations. Such direct, causative evidence is almost impossible to furnish. Slackening winds and post-monsoon atmospheric dryness are known to trap the latent particulate matter from vehicles, industries, construction dust and stubble burning. Crackers are only an additional element that further degrades an already vitiated air. Delhi’s five-day average AQI rose from approximately 298 before Deepavali to 358 afterwards in 2024, 259 to 315 in 2025 and from 350 to 376 in 2026. While the timing of these spikes is consistent with a contribution from firecrackers, their precise share of overall pollution cannot be isolated from other emissions and meteorological influences. An absolute ban would encourage “illegal crackers from across the border,” the Court was told. Cracker season begins a fortnight before Deepavali and therefore an earlier decision by the Court regarding its permissibility would have given stockists time to better dispense ‘green’ crackers.

However, it is important to note that CSIR-NEERI, the developers of the products, underline that low-emission crackers — under stringent lab conditions — only reduce emissions by 30%–45%. These percentage reductions reveal nothing about gross particulate matter emissions. The post-Deepavali AQI is evidence of this. The Court acknowledges, but does not address, the immense implementation challenges in policing cracker sales and hyphenates crackers with religious observation but pays only lip service to provisions in the Constitution that say that religious customs cannot override considerations of health and life. Rather than wait for the week running up to Deepavali 2027, the Court must pronounce a final view on crackers and lay down the contours for the government to evolve a policy on limiting the manufacture, sale, and burning of crackers in a time-bound manner.

articles.title: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision to invite opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government reflects the real mandate of the October 27 legislative elections. While Mr. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party finished second with 21 seats, behind Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud, which won 27, the former military chief, who campaigned on an anti-Netanyahu platform, has secured the support of 67 legislators in the 120-member Knesset. In Mr. Eisenkot’s own words, Israel risks “descending to dark places, to a point of no return”. But it is not yet clear what kind of a government Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to form. The opposition parties are split between a Jewish-led bloc with 48 MKs and an Arab-led bloc of 19 MKs. Arab parties have offered in-principle support for Mr. Eisenkot to keep Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition out of power. But what is not clear is whether they would be part of the government or offer outside support by allowing Mr. Eisenkot to run a minority government. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s Jewish right-wing allies, such as Avigdor Lieberman, are opposed to joining hands with Arab parties. Mr. Eisenkot has now called for a unity government, appealing even to Likud and the far-right Religious Zionism, to join him.

But the challenges facing Israel’s next leader are formidable and immediate. Mr. Netanyahu’s unchecked militarism has deepened Israel’s international isolation, strained its relationship with the U.S., its most important patron and ally, and aggravated the security challenges it faces in its neighbourhood. At home, the surge of the far-right has further polarised society, while systemic violence against Palestinians has spread across the West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu’s response to these challenges has been to unleash more violence, which has only compounded Israel’s problems. If Mr. Eisenkot is serious about pulling Israel back from the point of no return, he must pursue a three-pronged approach. Firstly, he should form an Arab-Jewish unity government focused on healing the country’s internal wounds and bridging gaps between communities. Second, Israel’s deepening international isolation and increasingly negative public opinion around the world will begin to exact a heavy toll sooner rather than later. Tel Aviv must take urgent steps to restore its international standing. Third, Israel must reopen the path to peace. The new government should initiate negotiations with the Palestinians under international mediation, crack down on settler violence, pull back from Gaza and reaffirm its commitment to the two-state solution. Without peace, Israel risks continuing to “descend to dark places”.
